recipe: Expect that unmounting a component destroys all of its state, so plan for re-initialization when you conditionally add it back to the tree.
trigger_condition: You are conditionally rendering a stateful component (e.g., via a boolean flag) and need to know what happens to its state when it is removed and re-added.
evidence: Notice how the moment you stop rendering the second counter, its state disappears completely. That's because when React removes a component, it destroys its state.
source_name: react.dev learn: Preserving and Resetting State

recipe: Always declare component functions at the top level; never define a component function inside another component's body, because each render creates a new function identity and React will reset all state below it.
trigger_condition: You are defining a helper component function inside the body of a parent component.
evidence: always declare component functions at the top level, and don't nest their definitions.
source_name: react.dev learn: Preserving and Resetting State

recipe: To reset a component's state when switching between logically separate instances, render them in different positions in the tree so React treats them as distinct nodes rather than the same node with changed props.
trigger_condition: Two logically separate components appear in the same UI position and you need their state to be independent.
evidence: If you want these two `Counter`s to be independent, you can render them in two different positions
source_name: react.dev learn: Preserving and Resetting State

recipe: Give each component an explicit identity with the key prop to force React to treat them as separate instances and reset their state when switching between them.
trigger_condition: You need to reset state at the same position in the tree and cannot restructure the tree to use different positions.
evidence: Give each component an explicit identity with `key`
source_name: react.dev learn: Preserving and Resetting State

recipe: Use a `key` prop to force React to treat components as distinct, resetting their state when the key changes.
trigger_condition: When you need a component to reset its state each time it is re-rendered, such as switching between different users or form targets.
evidence: You can force a subtree to reset its state by giving it a different key.
source_name: react.dev learn: Preserving and Resetting State

recipe: Don't define component functions inside other component functions, as this creates new component types on every render and resets state accidentally.
trigger_condition: When writing React components that contain state.
evidence: Don't nest component definitions, or you'll reset state by accident.
source_name: react.dev learn: Preserving and Resetting State

recipe: When you have only a few independent components rendered in the same place, render them separately in JSX to keep their state independent.
trigger_condition: When you have a small number of independent components that should not share state.
evidence: This solution is convenient when you only have a few independent components rendered in the same place.
source_name: react.dev learn: Preserving and Resetting State

recipe: Provide a changing `key` to a React element to force React to re-create its DOM node from scratch instead of reusing and updating it in place.
trigger_condition: When you need an element to fully reset (e.g., clearing a stale image before the next one loads) rather than being updated in place.
evidence: You can provide a `key` to the `` tag. When that `key` changes, React will re-create the `` DOM node from scratch.
source_name: react.dev learn: Preserving and Resetting State

recipe: Use a stable unique identifier (such as an item's `id` field) as the `key` when mapping over a list, rather than the array index.
trigger_condition: When the order of a rendered list can change (e.g., sorting or reversing) and each item holds its own local state.
